Issues.Title: XpsDocumentWriter.WriteAsync blocks the calling (UI) thread after the last page while Windows waits for the print job to complete
Issues.Body:
### Description

When a WPF app prints with the documented pattern, `PrintDialog` and then `XpsDocumentWriter.WriteAsync` from the UI thread, the pages are
written asynchronously and the UI stays responsive while they are. After the last page, though, the UI thread is blocked until the print job
has been committed by Windows. For a large document this is tens of seconds: about 23 s for 1,260 pages to "Microsoft Print to PDF" on our test VM. During
that time the window doesn't repaint or respond to input, and Windows may show it as "Not Responding".

From process dumps (taken while the write ran on a separate STA thread; see "Other information"), the block is inside `WriteAsync`'s completion: `IXpsOMPackageWriter.Close` calls `winspool!EndDocPrinter`, which waits
for the job in `winspool!WaitForJobCompletion`, a `Sleep` loop, on the thread that called `WriteAsync`. The `XpsDocumentWriter`
documentation (`WriteAsync`, `WritingCompleted`) doesn't mention a blocking wait after the pages are written, so an app has no reason to
expect it.

### Reproduction Steps

Source: https://gist.github.com/markabrandjord/99ad9cde5c591501aa664f39f354942c

A minimal WPF app (one window, about 400 lines plus a 150-line COM interop file). The window has a clock that ticks every 100 ms, a page count,
**Print (problem)** and **Print (solution)** buttons, and a status line that reports when the last page was written, when the print
finished, and the longest gap between two clock ticks. It ends with a verdict: `FROZE: the UI thread was blocked for N s` when the
longest gap is over 1 s, otherwise `OK`. The same line is also written to the console and to `Trace` (the debugger's Output window).

The problem path is the documented pattern:

```csharp
var dialog = new PrintDialog();
if (dialog.ShowDialog() == true)
{
    XpsDocumentWriter writer = PrintQueue.CreateXpsDocumentWriter(dialog.PrintQueue);
    writer.WritingProgressChanged += ...; // records the time of the last FixedPageWritingProgress
    writer.WritingCompleted += ...;      // records the time it is raised, and the longest clock gap
    writer.WriteAsync(paginator, dialog.PrintTicket); // paginator: 1,000+ simple text pages
}
```

1. Build and run the app (`dotnet run -f net10.0-windows -c Release`).
2. Leave the page count at 1,000 or more.
3. Click **Print (problem)**, choose **Microsoft Print to PDF**, click Print, and choose a file name in Windows' "Save Print Output As" box.
4. Watch the clock after the last page has been written.

### Expected behavior

The UI thread stays responsive for the whole print, including the time Windows takes to finish the job, and `WritingCompleted` is raised
when the job is done.

### Actual behavior

The clock ticks while the pages are written, then stops after the last page and stays stopped until `WritingCompleted` is raised. The
status line shows a clock gap of the same length as the time between the last page and `WritingCompleted`, and ends with `FROZE`, e.g.:

```
Problem printed: last page progress at 19.5 s, WritingCompleted at 42.8 s (23.3 s after the last page); longest clock gap 23.3 s. FROZE: the UI thread was blocked for 23.3 s (a clock gap over 1 s counts as frozen).
```

Measured with the attached app on a Windows 11 x64 VM with .NET 10, 1,260 pages to Microsoft Print to PDF, with a hang probe (`WM_NULL`
sent to the window every 250 ms) and UI Automation reads of the status line running throughout:

| Approach | Runs | Longest clock gap | Longest hang probe | The app's verdict | Froze? |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Documented pattern (`WriteAsync` on the UI thread) | 3 | 23.3 s, 23.3 s, 23.4 s | 23.2 s, 23.2 s, 23.2 s | `FROZE` in every run | Every run |
| Workaround below | 3 | 0.3 s, 0.2 s, 0.2 s | 101 ms, 164 ms, 221 ms | `OK` in every run | Never |

All six PDFs had all 1,260 pages. In the workaround runs, `Close` returned 22.0 s after the last page went into the job, which is the
same wait, on a thread nothing else needs.

The same wait is visible in the workaround, where it is harmless: in the attached app's headless check (`--selfcheck 200`) on a Windows 11
desktop with .NET 10, `IXpsOMPackageWriter.Close` returned 5.9 s after the last page of a 200-page job went into it.

### Regression?

Not known. We haven't tested .NET Framework or earlier .NET versions.

### Known Workarounds

Keep the job-commit wait off the UI thread, and off any STA thread:

1. On the UI thread: `PrintDialog` for the printer and ticket. For a file printer (port `PORTPROMPT:`), the app shows its own
   `SaveFileDialog` and keeps the chosen path.
2. On a new STA thread: serialize the pages with `XpsDocument.CreateXpsDocumentWriter(xpsDocument).Write(paginator, ticket)` into an XPS
   package in a temporary file. No print queue is involved, so nothing waits on the print system here.
3. On a new MTA thread that owns no windows: `IPrintDocumentPackageTargetFactory::CreateDocumentPackageTargetForPrintJob` (printer name, job
   name, the output file as the job output stream, the ticket), then `IXpsDocumentPackageTarget::GetXpsOMFactory`, load the package with
   `IXpsOMObjectFactory::CreatePackageFromStream`, copy its pages into the target's `IXpsOMPackageWriter` (`StartNewDocument`, `AddPage`),
   and call `Close`.

Why this works: `Close` still waits for the job, but on a thread that no window, message pump or other COM apartment depends on. Because
the output file is passed as the job output stream, Windows' own "Save Print Output As" box never shows, so no print-system window is
created on any worker thread either.

The cost is real: about 150 lines of COM interop for an API that WPF already wraps, and the app loses `XpsDocumentWriter`'s direct
`PrintQueue` path.

### Impact

Any WPF app that prints large documents with the documented pattern freezes for the length of the job commit, which grows with the page
count. Users see a "Not Responding" window at the end of a print that otherwise looked asynchronous. Assistive technology loses access to the
window for that time.

### Configuration

- Windows 11 Pro x64 (10.0.26300), and a Windows 11 x64 test VM.
- .NET 10 (10.0.14 locally). The attached project also targets `net8.0-windows` and builds cleanly for it. The .NET 8 build was run only on
  the .NET 10 runtime (`DOTNET_ROLL_FORWARD=Major`), since no .NET 8 desktop runtime was installed.
- Printer: Microsoft Print to PDF. We expect other printers to behave alike, since the wait is in winspool's job completion, but we only
  measured this one.

### Other information

**Root cause as we understand it** (from process dumps read with `dotnet-dump` and native frames resolved with Microsoft's public symbols;
we have no access to the source of the native parts):

The dumps were taken in a larger app that ran the write on a separate STA thread with its own `Dispatcher` (see the secondary effect below); we have not dumped the UI-thread case. There, the thread that called `WriteAsync` was blocked in this chain, in a dispatcher item after the last page. The UI-thread freeze measured above matches it in timing: the window stops answering at the last page and resumes when `WritingCompleted` is raised.

```
XpsOMSerializationManagerAsync.OnXPSSerializationCompleted
 -> XpsDocumentWriter.ForwardWriteCompletedEvent
 -> PrintQueue.DisposeSerializationManager
 -> XpsCompatiblePrinter.EndDocPrinter
 -> IXpsOMPackageWriter.Close
 -> XpsPrint!XpsPrint::XpsPackageConsumerXPS::Close
 -> XpsPrint!TXpsPrintWorkItemXPSOM::Close
 -> winspool!EndDocPrinter
 -> winspool!WaitForJobCompletion
 -> KERNELBASE!Sleep        (a polling loop until the job completes)
```

So `WritingCompleted` is raised only after the job has completed, and the wait happens synchronously on the calling thread without pumping
messages.

**A secondary effect (an observation from a larger app; the attached repro doesn't reproduce it).** Microsoft's "How to print an XPS file"
sample runs the write on a separate STA thread with its own `Dispatcher`, which is also the obvious fix for the freeze above. The UI thread
then stays responsive, but that STA is still blocked in the same `WaitForJobCompletion` loop without pumping. In a larger app, dumps showed
UI Automation's server thread in the app's process waiting on a cross-apartment COM call (`ReleaseCollection::DispatchReleases` releasing
UIA proxies such as `MiniHwndProxy`) into that blocked STA. Every request from that UI Automation client queued behind it, so UI Automation
reads of the app's (responsive) main window, from a test client and from a screen reader, took up to about 19 s to answer, and were all
answered together the moment the job completed. The proxies were most likely for Windows' "Save Print Output As" box, which a file printer
shows on the thread that starts the job. Our standalone repro didn't show this stall, so we can't give a minimal repro for it; we mention it because it means moving `WriteAsync` to another STA thread isn't a complete fix.

**Suggested fix.** Do the job-commit wait in a way that doesn't block the calling STA: for example, perform the `Close`/`EndDocPrinter` on a
worker MTA thread and marshal `WritingCompleted` back to the caller's dispatcher afterwards, or wait for the job completion asynchronously
(or with a pumping wait) instead of in winspool's `Sleep` loop. Failing that, documenting that `WriteAsync` blocks the calling thread until
the job has completed would help apps plan for it.

Issues.Title: WPF build fails with MSB3030 when NuGet dependency graph spec writing is disabled
Issues.Body:
### Description

With `RestoreDoNotWriteDependencyGraphSpec=true` set, NuGet restore no longer writes `obj/<project>.nuget.dgspec.json` files. The option was added in https://github.com/NuGet/Home/issues/14114 but [Microsoft.WinFX.targets](https://github.com/dotnet/wpf/blob/49ae5cd6e0ba39eb9d54b93e35af6a0bfe0b7d51/src/Microsoft.DotNet.Wpf/src/PresentationBuildTasks/Microsoft.WinFX.targets#L391) still unconditionally copies the file, which raises an MSB3030 error.

### Reproduction Steps

1. Install .NET SDK 10.0.4xx
2. Create a WPF Project: `dotnet new wpf -n test`
3. Add this to the project file:
```xml
<PropertyGroup>
  <RestoreDoNotWriteDependencyGraphSpec>true</RestoreDoNotWriteDependencyGraphSpec>
</PropertyGroup>
```
4. Run `dotnet build`

### Expected behavior

The build should succeed, and the restore skips writing `*.nuget.dgspec.json` files.

### Actual behavior

MSB3030 error:

C:\Program Files\dotnet\sdk\10.0.403\Sdks\Microsoft.NET.Sdk.WindowsDesktop\targets\Microsoft.WinFX.targets(408,7): error MSB3030: Could not copy the file "...\test\obj\WpfDgspecRepro.csproj.nuget.dgspec.json" because it was not found.


### Regression?

This wouldn't have failed before the option to disable dependency graph writing was introduced in SDK 10.0.4xx

### Known Workarounds

I turned the property off for WPF projects only but this results in some dgspec files still being written.

### Impact

RestoreDoNotWriteDependencyGraphSpec can't be adopted repo-wide without compilation errors.

### Configuration

Windows 11 x64, .NET 10.0.403

### Other information

_No response_

Issues.Title: Retarget WPF to .NET 12
Issues.Body:
Fixes # <!-- Issue Number -->

Main PR <!-- Link to PR if any that fixed this in the main branch. -->

## Description

Retargets WPF to .NET 12 as part of the .NET 12 TFM update.

- `Directory.Build.props`: `TargetFramework` `net11.0` → `net12.0`, `TargetFrameworkVersion` `11.0` → `12.0`.
- `Documentation/developer-guide.md`: sample uses `net12.0-windows`.
- Project template changes will be in a follow-up PR.

`Microsoft.WinFX.targets` still loads PresentationBuildTasks from `tools\net11.0`, because the task is built for `$(BundledNETCoreAppTargetFramework)`, which is still `net11.0` with the current SDK. It should move when the SDK bundles net12.0.

## Customer Impact

Without this change, WPF continues to build against net11.0 while the rest of the .NET 12 stack has moved to net12.0.

## Regression

No.

## Testing

Local, Debug x64:
- `.\eng\scripts\cibuild.cmd -configuration Debug /p:Platform=x64 /p:Coverage=false`: passed, 0 warnings, 0 errors.
- `.\eng\scripts\ciunittest.cmd -configuration Debug /p:Platform=x64 /p:Coverage=false`: all 6 unit-test projects passed on `.NETCoreApp,Version=v12.0`, 0 failures.

## Risk

Low. Only the root target framework changes; build and unit tests pass.

Issues.Title: [release/10.0] Restore WPF clipboard text auto conversion for managed data objects
Issues.Body:
Fixes #11968 

## Description

Restores Windows clipboard text auto conversion for WPF after the .NET 10 migration to shared OLE code.

WPF opts into a captured native fallback for Text , UnicodeText, and OEMText , while preserving managed custom-payload identity. Plain-text availability reflects Windows’ published clipboard formats, and convenience getters remain compatible with legacy IDataObject implementations.

Requires the corresponding shared-core changes in dotnet/winforms and an updated Microsoft.Private.Winforms dependency.

## Customer Impact

Applications publishing ANSI text can incorrectly receive false from Clipboard.ContainsText() or empty text from Clipboard.GetText(), breaking clipboard workflows that worked in .NET 9.

## Regression

Yes. Fixes a .NET 10 regression in clipboard text conversion.

## Testing

Added coverage for native text synthesis before and after flushing, disabled managed conversion, published-format availability, typed and legacy retrieval, custom-payload identity, and RTF negative controls.

Validation used the matching local shared-core package:

## Risk

Moderate. Native fallback is restricted to three plain-text formats and enabled only for WPF; unrelated formats retain their existing retrieval paths, and WinForms remains opted out.

Issues.Title: Namespaces in generated files g.cs and g.i.cs may be interpreted as relative namespace instead of absolute namespace
Issues.Body:
### Description

If a generated file from a UserControl in the namespace B.A references any type from the namespace A, the compiler will assume that the type is in the namespace B.A, not A. This will make the compilation fail.


### Reproduction Steps

Add these three files in your Wpf project, and try to compile it. The compiler will assume that `CustomTextBlock` is in the namespace `B.A` instead of `A`.

CustomTextBlock.cs
```csharp
using System.Windows.Controls;

namespace A
{
    public class CustomTextBlock : TextBlock
    {
    }
}
```

MyUserControl.xaml
```xaml
<UserControl x:Class="B.A.MyUserControl"
             xmlns="http://schemas.microsoft.com/winfx/2006/xaml/presentation"
             xmlns:x="http://schemas.microsoft.com/winfx/2006/xaml"
             xmlns:a="clr-namespace:A">
    <a:CustomTextBlock x:Name="MyTextBlock"/>
</UserControl>
```

MyUserControl.xaml.cs
```csharp
using System.Windows.Controls;

namespace B.A
{
    public partial class MyUserControl : UserControl
    {
        public MyUserControl()
        {
            InitializeComponent();
        }
    }
}
```


### Expected behavior

Project should be able to compile.

### Actual behavior

Project does not compile. The compilation error states that `CustomTextBlock` does not exist in the namespace `B.A`.

### Regression?

I don't think so but I only tested in .NET 10.

### Known Workarounds

Either:
 - change one of the namespace (if you can)
 - use a "proxy" class that inherits the type from A but in a different namespace


### Impact

This will make the compilation fail, unless we use one of the aforementionned workarounds.

### Configuration

Windows 11 x64, .NET 10.0.403


### Other information

In non-generated files, we can work around this by using the `global` namespace alias as documented here: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/operators/namespace-alias-qualifier. Could this be used in the auto generated files ?
